title: Reverse Integer
statement: Reverse the decimal digits of a signed 32-bit integer and keep its sign. If the reversed number does not fit in the signed 32-bit range, return 0. Do not rely on a wider integer type to hold the answer.

example.caption: -123 reversed is -321. The sign stays where it is.

idea.sentence: Peel the last digit off x with % 10, push it onto result with result * 10 + digit, and check against the 32-bit limit before the multiply.

jargon.plain: -2147483648 to 2147483647. A reversed number outside it counts as overflow, and the answer is 0.
Drop the fraction. -12.3 becomes -12, not -13. Go and C do this for integer division.
Test result against the limit divided by 10 first. After the multiply it is too late if the type wrapped.

watch.inputHint: One argument: an integer, e.g. 123 or -120

vars.meaning: number of decimal digits (at most 10 here)

rows.name: String reverse
rows.note: Convert to text, reverse it, parse it back, then range-check the parsed value.

rows.name: Peel and push
rows.note: One turn per digit and a single integer. The limit check happens inside the loop.

fast.takeaway: Both are O(d), but the digit loop needs no text and no big integer. The detail that matters is where you put the overflow check.

stages.title: Set the limit
stages.note: result starts at 0. The limit is 214748364, one tenth of the largest int32.

stages.title: Peel a digit
stages.note: x % 10 is the last digit with the sign of x. Dividing by 10 toward zero drops it.

stages.title: Check, then push
stages.note: If result * 10 + digit would leave the int32 range, return 0. Otherwise push the digit.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: x is 0, so every digit has moved. result holds the reversed number.

edges.title: Trailing zeros vanish
edges.why: The 0 is peeled first and becomes a leading zero of the result, which is no digit at all.

edges.title: Overflow gives 0
edges.why: The reverse is 9646324351, bigger than 2147483647. The check fires when result is 964632435.

edges.title: Negative minimum
edges.why: Its reverse, -8463847412, is below the smallest int32. Note x itself is valid input.

edges.title: Zero
edges.why: The loop never runs. The answer is 0.

gotchas.text: Numbers are doubles, so result * 10 + digit never wraps. You must still check the 32-bit range yourself, or 1534236469 returns 9646324351 instead of 0.
x / 10 is a float division. Use Math.trunc(x / 10). Math.floor is wrong for negatives: floor(-12.3) is -13. And x % 10 keeps the sign, so -123 % 10 is -3.
Do not 'fix' overflow with result | 0. It wraps silently into a wrong negative number instead of returning 0.

Go's / truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the dividend, like JS. Python differs: -123 // 10 is -13. Go's int is 64-bit, so it will not overflow for 32-bit input but the range check is still required.
The two limits differ by one: the largest int32 ends in 7 and the smallest in -8. The check on the last digit has to use 7 for positives and -8 for negatives.

recap.key: digit = x % 10, x = trunc(x / 10), result = result * 10 + digit, and return 0 if result is already past one tenth of the limit.
recap.complexity: Time O(d) for d digits, at most 10. Space O(1).
moves: Peel digit = x % 10 and drop it from x
If result > 214748364 (or equal and digit > 7), return 0
Same for the negative side with -8
